settings.text: It helped for ten minutes. Then she was back at the microwave for the fourth time that night.

settings.title: The creams.
settings.text: Warm on the skin, nothing in the joint, and it came off on her trousers.

settings.text: Lovely woman. Six sessions, a sheet of exercises, and a ten-week wait to be seen again.

settings.heading: What Paula tried
settings.intro: The cupboard filled up. The knee stayed the same.
settings.belief: None of it failed because her knee was too far gone. It failed because every one of them gives you warmth that fades.

settings.title: Warmth, held at the level you set
settings.text: Five levels from 45°C to 65°C. Pick one and it stays there for the whole half hour, instead of starting hot and fading like a wheat bag. Most people sit at 45 to 50°C: start low, wear it over clothing, and only go higher if it stays comfortable.

settings.title: Gentle massage, running alongside
settings.text: Three strengths, or none. It runs at the same time as the warmth, so you are not holding anything or rubbing anything in.

settings.title: Strapped on, cordless, off by itself
settings.text: It stays where you put it while you walk to the kettle. No wire. At 30 minutes it switches itself off, so it cannot be left running.

settings.heading: How it works
settings.intro: Targeted deep heat and massage, held on the joint for a full thirty minutes.

settings.heading: What the NHS says about heat
settings.intro: Not us. Published guidance, with the source so you can read it yourself.
settings.footnote: Jointwell is a comfort device. It is not a medical treatment and does not cure, treat or prevent any condition. Keep doing what your GP and physio have told you to do.

settings.role: nhs.uk, on easing joint stiffness at home
settings.quote: Heat applied to the affected area can be very effective in reducing pain.

settings.text: Heat-pack guidance says apply warmth for 15 to 20 minutes. A hot water bottle holds useful warmth for 20 to 30 minutes and a microwaved wheat bag about 30. The dose in your cupboard is roughly right. It is the delivery that runs out.
Knees, shoulders and elbows sit under thin skin with little muscle or fat around them, so they lose warmth faster than the rest of you and hold it worst. Cold hands, cold nose, cold knees.

NICE, which writes the guidance the NHS follows, puts exercise, weight management and information first for osteoarthritis. We are not a substitute for any of that. Warmth is what people use to get moving in the morning so they can do the rest.
settings.source: NICE guideline NG226, Osteoarthritis in over 16s (2022)

settings.name: Sarah
settings.quote: I set it to 45 and it stays at 45. That's the whole difference from the hot water bottle I used before, which was lovely for 20 minutes and then a cold lump. I do half an hour on my shoulder after lunch and I'm not stiff reaching for things on the top shelf anymore.

settings.name: Margaret
settings.quote: Bought it for my knee, ended up using it on my shoulder more. The strap holds it in place so I can sit with a cup of tea and forget it's there. My physio said heat and gentle massage was worth trying and this does both without me having to hold it on.

settings.name: Linda
settings.quote: No cable, which matters more than I expected. I wear it in my chair by the window and don't have to sit near a socket. A charge lasts me 4 sessions. It's not a cure, my knee is 70 years old, but getting down the stairs first thing is better than it was.

settings.name: Brenda
settings.quote: I wear it over my trousers while I do the crossword and it's warm enough to feel through the fabric. The massage is firmer than I expected and you can turn it down. Only thing I'd say is the strap takes a minute to get right the first time.

settings.name: Susan
settings.quote: I'm not good with gadgets and I was worried. There are four buttons and a number. Up, down, that's it. My daughter set the timer for me once and I've managed on my own since. I've ordered two more for my sister and neighbour.

settings.title: Knee arthritis
settings.line: Wear and tear, the GP says. The first ten steps are the worst and the stairs are a decision.
settings.how: Straight round the knee, over or under trousers. The strap holds it while you walk to the kettle.
settings.when: First thing, with the first cup. Level 3, thirty minutes, before the stairs.
settings.note: Heat before you move, ice after a flare. That is what physios say, and it is all we say.
settings.alt: Woman at the kettle with the wrap on her knee

settings.title: Stiff shoulder
settings.line: The top shelf, the bra strap, sleeping on that side. Small things, twenty times a day.
settings.how: The extension strap in the box loops it over the shoulder and under the arm, so the warm panel sits on the joint.
settings.when: Under a cardigan while the tea brews, and again in the armchair in the evening.
settings.note: A wheat bag slides off a shoulder. This one stays.
settings.alt: Woman in an armchair with the wrap on her shoulder

settings.title: Tennis elbow
settings.line: From the secateurs and the watering can, not the tennis court. Worse when you grip.
settings.how: The strap takes it up the forearm to the elbow. Rest the arm on the chair and forget it.
settings.when: Before the garden, not after. Twenty to thirty minutes on the forearm as a warm-up.
settings.note: If the elbow is hot and sore to touch after a session, that is an ice day.
settings.alt: Woman doing a crossword with the wrap on her elbow

settings.title: After a knee replacement
settings.line: Ask your surgeon or physio first. Their word beats ours.
settings.how: Only once the wound has fully healed and they have said heat is fine. Start at the lowest level.
settings.when: The warm half hour before the exercise sheet, then the exercises.
settings.note: Never over a wound that has not healed, and never on a hot, red or newly swollen knee. That is a phone call to the clinic.
settings.alt: Woman at the breakfast table with the wrap on her knee

settings.title: Morning stiffness
settings.line: Hand on the wall, down the stairs sideways, fine by the afternoon. Then tomorrow.
settings.how: On the worst joint before you leave the kitchen. Kettle on, wrap on.
settings.when: Every morning for a month. Same chair, same cup. Habit is the whole trick.
settings.note: A joint that has not moved for eight hours is a cold joint. Warmth and movement are what wake it.
settings.alt: Woman by the window with the wrap on her knee

settings.title: Kneeling and gardening
settings.line: It is not the kneeling. It is getting down, and getting back up.
settings.how: Round the knee before the wellies go on. It is cordless, so it goes to the back door with you.
settings.when: Twenty minutes before you go out, and again in the chair when you come in.
settings.note: Two knees? Two wraps. The pair is the one most gardeners choose.
settings.alt: Woman on the carpet with the wrap on her knee

settings.title: Cold weather aches
settings.line: October to March. Some knees know the weather before the curtains are open.
settings.how: Under a dressing gown while the kettle boils, in the armchair with the television, in the car before a cold walk.
settings.when: Morning and evening on the coldest days. One charge covers the day for most people.
settings.note: One knee warm, not the whole house. The heating can stay where it is.
settings.alt: Woman in an armchair by the radiator with the wrap on her knee

settings.intro: Straight answers. If yours is not here, ring us.

settings.question: Isn't this just a heating pad with extra steps?
settings.answer: A heating pad gives you heat that fades, or heat that ties you to a wall socket. Jointwell holds whichever of the five levels you pick, 45°C to 65°C, for a full 30 minutes. It adds vibration massage at three strengths, straps on so it stays put, and runs cordless in any chair in the house.

settings.question: Will it work for me? My joints have been like this a long time.
settings.answer: It isn't a cure and we won't pretend otherwise. Nobody can promise what it will do for your joint. What we can promise is warmth at the level you choose, held for thirty minutes, with massage alongside it. The 90-day trial is there so your own knee gets the deciding vote rather than our copy.

settings.question: Will it fit me?
settings.answer: One size, 46 cm across and 30 cm tall, with a 55 cm strap span. It fits either knee, and the extension strap in the box takes it round a shoulder or up an arm to the elbow. If it doesn't fit you, the 90-day trial covers a full refund and we pay the return postage.

settings.question: Is it safe? Will it burn me?
settings.answer:
Heat can burn skin if it is too hot, held too long, or used by someone who cannot feel it properly. So: start at level 1 or 2 (45 to 50°C), wear it over clothing rather than bare skin, and only go higher if it stays comfortable. Every session ends itself after 30 minutes, so it cannot be left running, and you can stop it at any point.

Do not use it while asleep, over broken skin, or on a joint that is hot, red and swollen. If you have diabetes, circulation problems, reduced feeling in your skin, or you are under medical care for that joint, ask your GP before using any heat product. If the skin goes red and stays red after you take it off, that level is too high for you.

settings.question: When will it arrive?
settings.answer: We dispatch within 1 to 3 working days and most orders arrive within 7 to 10 working days of ordering, occasionally up to 14. Every order is tracked and we email you the link the moment it leaves us.

settings.question: How do I know this isn't another Facebook gadget?
settings.answer: Fair question, because this market is full of them. We dispatch most orders within 1 to 3 working days and track every one. There's a UK returns address, UK support, a 2-year warranty, and a 90-day trial where we pay the postage back. The reviews on this page are from customers with an order on file, in their own words. Junk sellers can't afford the guarantee.

settings.question: Can I use it after a knee replacement?
settings.answer: Ask your surgeon or physio first, and follow what they say. Many people are told heat is fine once the wound has fully healed, but that is their call, not ours. If they say yes, most people use it as the warm half hour before their exercises.

settings.question: How do I charge it, and how long does a charge last?
settings.answer: It charges over USB-C with the cable in the box, the same cable as most phones. It has a 3000 mAh battery. The panel shows the battery level.

settings.question: What happens if I send it back?
settings.answer: Email us within 90 days of delivery. We send you a UK returns address and a postage label. Post it back, and we refund what you paid in full once it arrives. You do not pay the postage and you do not have to give a reason, though we would like to hear it.

settings.question: Who shouldn't use it?
settings.answer: Anyone who has been told to avoid heat on that joint. If you have diabetes, circulation problems, reduced feeling in your skin, a pacemaker, an unhealed wound or a joint that is hot, red and swollen, talk to your GP before using any heat product. Do not use it while asleep, over broken skin, or on a child. If you are pregnant or under medical care for the joint, ask first. It is a comfort device, not a treatment, and your GP's word beats ours.

settings.heading: It starts with the stairs. It never stays there.
settings.intro: If any of this sounds familiar, keep reading.

settings.shot: Stairs, shot from the bottom looking up. Hand on the banister in the corner of frame.
settings.lines:
Sideways?
One step at a time?
Maybe even on your hands and knees?

settings.shot: Armchair, side-on. A woman leaning forward, hand on the arm, about to stand.
settings.lines:
You work out how you'll get up before you've sat down.
It used to be where you relaxed.

settings.shot: Open car door in a supermarket car park. One foot on the ground, one still inside.
settings.lines:
That pause before you put your weight on it.
Hoping nobody's watching.

settings.shot: Overgrown garden through a kitchen window. Mug on the sill.
settings.lines:
Too much kneeling.
Too much bending.
You don't want it to, but the grass gets longer every day.

settings.shot: Dark bedroom, someone lying on their back, ceiling.
settings.lines:
You've stopped sleeping on that side.
Then the other side started too.

Everyone your age has a knee.
So you don't mention it.
You just plan around it.

settings.heading: Then you go to the GP.
settings.intro: Everyone does their best. It still is not enough.

settings.shot: GP waiting room. Row of chairs, the ticket screen, a poster about flu jabs.
settings.lines:
You put it off. It's only a knee.
When you finally go, you get eight minutes.

settings.shot: A hand pressing on a knee. Clinical, close, cropped.
settings.lines:
Wear and tear, they say.
Very common.
Paracetamol, keep it moving, lose a bit if you can.

settings.shot: A brown NHS envelope on a doormat.
settings.lines:
The physio letter takes ten weeks.
Six sessions.
A sheet of exercises for the landing carpet.

settings.shot: Printed exercise sheet, folded, on a kitchen table. Coffee ring on it.
settings.lines:
The physio is lovely.
The exercises hurt.
By session four you've stopped, and neither of you mentions it.

settings.shot: A syringe on a tray, out of focus.
settings.lines:
So it's the injection.
And it works. Properly works.
For about ten weeks.

settings.shot: A calendar page with a date circled.
settings.lines:
Then one morning it's back.
"We can only do that a few times a year."
"Have you thought about a replacement?"

Referred. Not booked.
A letter. A consultation. A list.
Nobody says how long the list is.
You look it up and wish you hadn't.

settings.shot: Three boxes on a bedside table. Co-codamol, naproxen, paracetamol. Labels visible.
settings.lines:
One leaves you foggy.
One upsets your stomach.
One is fine. It's just not enough any more.

None of this is anyone's fault.
The GP has eight minutes. The physio has six sessions. The surgeon has a list.
It's just that nobody's job is to get you up the stairs this month.

settings.text: That's the bit Paula got tired of waiting for.

settings.quote: I found it in a Facebook group for osteoarthritis. At first I was sceptical. Was it really going to do anything? I had already tried the lot. Then I saw the 90-day guarantee, a 90-day trial they called it: if it doesn't work, send it back. So I thought, go on then, what is there to lose.

settings.lines:
Properly warm, right into the joint. The squeezing I wasn't expecting. It was like someone's hands.
It felt good while it was on.
I'd had nice before, though.

I'd started doing it first thing, on the edge of the bed with the radio on.
The mornings weren't as stiff.
I put it down to the weather.

I went up the stairs with the washing and didn't hold on.
I only noticed at the top.
I stood there a bit.

I did the borders in the garden. Not all of them.
But you could tell from the kitchen window.

Thirty minutes, first thing, same as brushing my teeth.
My sister asked what I'd been doing differently.
That's when I told her about the gadget.

Thirty minutes with it on, whenever it suited her, and she got on with her day.
If you recognised the stairs, the chair, the garden through the window, you're where she was at the start.
The device is the same one she's still using.
